title: Thermal-mechanical coupling failure analysis and optimization of an exhaust manifold
author: Haiqiang, Hao, et al.

steps.title: Metallographic microscopy of fracture
steps.instruction: Prepare metallographic sections of the central and surface regions of fractured sample 1# and examine them with a metallographic microscope at 100 × and 400 × magnifications; record that graphite spheroidization exceeds 90 % and that the microstructure consists mainly of austenite, carbides, a few alloy phases and dendrites.

steps.title: SEM analysis of fracture morphology
steps.instruction: Observe the fracture surfaces with scanning electron microscopy: acquire images at 50 × (showing initiation and propagation zones with multi‑point initiation and intergranular traces) and at 400 × (showing tearing marks and visible cracking on the inner surface); conclude that the failure exhibits typical thermal‑fatigue features.

steps.title: Prepare tensile specimens
steps.instruction: Machine 15 tensile specimens from material QTANi35Si5Cr2 according to ASTM E21‑2020: each specimen 10 mm diameter, 100 mm gauge length, surface roughness Ra = 0.8 µm, with threads on both ends for clamping.

steps.title: High‑temperature tensile testing
steps.instruction: Using a universal tensile testing machine with heating capability, test the specimens at 20 °C and at high‑temperature steps of 300 °C, 500 °C and 700 °C (range 300‑700 °C). Set the cross‑head speed to 4 mm min⁻¹ and perform quasi‑static tension; record nominal stress‑strain curves, noting that at 300 °C the maximum stress increases slightly while strain rises by 150 %.

steps.title: Process tensile data
steps.instruction: Calculate material parameters from the averaged stress‑strain curves for each temperature. Record the values shown in Table 1:

steps.title: Build ABAQUS finite‑element model
steps.instruction: Create a solid‑element model of the exhaust manifold and its fixed bolts (numbers 1001‑1009) in ABAQUS using C3D4H (4‑node linear tetrahedron hybrid) elements; set the minimum casting fillet to 4 mm and the average element length to 2 mm, resulting in 148 445 tetrahedral elements. Model bolt‑to‑mounting‑hole connections with common nodes, generate triangular elements for closed inner and outer surfaces before tetrahedral meshing.

steps.title: Define temperature‑dependent material behavior
steps.instruction: Import five true stress‑strain curves (one for each temperature of interest) into ABAQUS, covering the material response from the yield point to rupture; these curves represent the material behavior at 20 °C, 300 °C, 500 °C, 600 °C and 700 °C.

steps.title: Apply mechanical load case
steps.instruction: Constrain all bolts (1001‑1009) to prevent translation along the coordinate axes. Apply static accelerations of x = 8 G, y = 10 G and z = 15 G to the manifold. Run a linear static analysis and note the maximum von Mises stress of 3.75 MPa on the outer surface, which is far below the material yield stress of ≈150 MPa at 700 °C.

steps.title: Apply thermal‑mechanical coupled loads
steps.instruction: Add thermal loads: set the outer surface temperature to 550 °C (engine speed 4000 rpm) and the inner surface temperature to 650 °C. Use a sequential coupling approach: (1) run the mechanical load step as above, (2) keep the mechanical loads and introduce the thermal loads while keeping bolt constraints. Run the coupled analysis and record the maximum von Mises stress of 150.7 MPa at the inner face of channel 1, with additional high stresses on the outer faces of channels 1‑3.

steps.title: Optimize bolt constraint configuration
steps.instruction: Modify bolt constraints: fully constrain bolts 1002, 1005 and 1008 (all three translational DOFs); constrain bolts 1001, 1003, 1004, 1006, 1007 and 1009 only in the x‑ and z‑directions. Re‑run the thermal‑mechanical coupled analysis. The resulting maximum von Mises stress is 145.2 MPa with a relatively uniform stress distribution. The manifold now has three fully constrained points and six points constrained in x and z directions, satisfying installation requirements.

description: The exhaust manifold is subjected to various loads, and the reasons for its failure may include structural design, material properties, working loads, and other factors. To study the causes and effects of exhaust manifold failure, this article conducts research on exhaust manifold manufacturing deviations, fracture morphology characteristics, material properties, working loads, and constraint boundary conditions. The method detail is organized as follows. The geometry inspection is presented in the next section. Fracture morphology and material properties are shown following geometry inspection. Finally, the finite element analysis is applied to study the effect of thermal load and constraint condition on the exhaust manifold. The aforementioned results indicate that the constraints in the x and z directions of the exhaust manifold are primarily due to installation requirements, while the constraint in the y direction is the main factor affecting thermal expansion stress. Base on this method, further detail analysis is applied to carry out better constraint position, constraint points and directions. A series analysis with constraints are applied to study exhaust manifold stress. The results show that constrained all the three-dimensional translational freedom at the bolts numbered 1002,1005 and 1008, and the bolts numbered 1001, 1003, 1004, 1006, 1007 and 1009 constrained the x and z-direction translational freedom can achieve more reasonable installation and stress distribution results. The maximum Von-Miese stress on the exhaust manifold is 145.2 MPa, and the stress distribution is relatively uniform throughout the exhaust manifold. The exhaust manifold has 3 fully constrained points and 6 constrained points in the x and z directions to ensure the installation requirements.
